{% include header.html %}

> V86 [/M:*size*] [*program* [*arguments*]]

Runs a real-mode *program* (a COM or EXE file, with `.COM` or `.EXE` added if *program* has no extension, found in the current directory, or if *program* has no drive or directory, in a directory of PATH$) in a V86 machine: memory that the program sees as an 8086 would, at addresses starting from 0, with the ROMs above it, while BASIC-DOS keeps running in protected mode.  Without a *program*, V86 runs COMMAND.COM, so `START V86` opens a real-mode command shell on a console of its own.  `/M:`*size* sets the machine's memory, in K, from 4 to 640 (eg, `START V86 /M:256` opens a shell in a 256K machine, and `START /B V86 /M:256 DEBUG` runs DEBUG in one without switching to its console); without it, the machine has 640K.  The machine uses that much of the system's memory for as long as it runs, however little its programs use, so a smaller *size* leaves more for other sessions.  Any switches after *program* are the program's own, but any other switch before it (or a *size* out of range) is a [usage error](../../#usage-errors).  V86 gets PATH$ the way an external program does, from its environment, but since a session that START makes has none, START gives V86 the current PATH$ ahead of its *arguments*, as it does for COMMAND.COM (eg, `START V86 DEBUG` runs `V86 PATH$="C:\;C:\EXT":DEBUG`), and V86 passes that PATH$ on to its program's environment, as PATH.

V86 machines need an 80386 (or later) running BASIC-DOS in protected mode with the 80386's features, which is the default (unless CONFIG.SYS has a `CPU=8088` or `CPU=80286` line; see [CPU](../../../cfg/#cpu)); otherwise, V86 displays `V86 mode not available`.  At a protected-mode prompt on such a machine, a real-mode EXE file fails with `Unable to load` and its name, followed by `Run START V86 first`: [START](../../system/#start) V86 opens a real-mode command shell that can run it (or `V86` *program* runs it on the current console).

The program can do anything an 8086 program can, except I/O (other than the ports listed below), and its interrupts and exceptions go to its own vectors, which it can hook (eg, with DOS function 25h).  V86 does the DOS functions that involve the machine itself (its vectors, memory blocks, PSPs, DTA, and running and ending programs, with their exit codes), and passes the rest of the DOS and BASIC-DOS functions on to BASIC-DOS, so the machine's files, consoles, and devices are V86's.  So COMMAND.COM runs in it as it does in real mode, along with the programs it runs (eg, BASIC-DOS's utilities, and tools like MASM and SYMDEB), with these differences:

- Floating-point works, through a copy of the FPU$ driver's functions in the machine's memory.
- The later programs of a pipeline (eg, MORE in `DIR | MORE`) run as ordinary BASIC-DOS programs, in sessions of their own, so a real-mode program can only be the first program of a pipeline.  START and KILL work as they do at any other prompt.
- MEM and FRE report the machine's memory, and so does the memory size in its BIOS data.
- [DEBUG](../debug/) works as it does in real mode, except that DM reports `?` (and LN finds no block), since the machine's memory blocks are V86's, not the CPU$ driver's.
- The common BIOS video (INT 10h), keyboard (INT 16h), and printer (INT 17h) functions work, but V86 does them with the console's own functions rather than the ROM's, so they work on any console (even a terminal, which can't read characters back from its screen, so programs that do, like MSBASIC, need a video console), and with its limits: a scrolled window is always as wide as the screen (though a character written at the end of the last row doesn't scroll it, as with the ROM), and a character that the console acts on (eg, RETURN) can't be drawn.  The functions are set mode, set cursor type and position, get cursor position, scroll up and down, read and write characters at the cursor, write teletype, and get mode; wait for a key and check for a key (and on a video console, the keyboard buffer and shift states in the machine's BIOS data stay current, for programs like MSBASIC that look there first); and print a character and get the printer's status.  The equipment (INT 11h), memory size (INT 12h), and tick count (INT 1Ah, function 00h) work, too, which the startup code of many C programs asks for, and on a VGA, so does INT 10h function 1Ah (get display combination), which is how programs know there's one.  Other BIOS functions do nothing.
- The machine gets timer ticks while its programs run: an INT 08h about 18 times a second, or as often as a program sets the timer's rate (counter 0, through ports 40h and 43h), up to about 1165 times a second, although they arrive in bursts after each of the system's ticks (ticks that are due while its interrupts are off wait until the next of the system's interrupts); the default INT 08h handler issues an INT 1Ch, as the ROM's does, and the tick count in its BIOS data stays current.  There are no ticks while a program waits in a DOS or BIOS function (eg, for a key).
- On a video console, a program that hooks INT 09h gets a keyboard interrupt for each scan code (key presses and releases) while its console has focus, one after each of the system's interrupts, and reads the code from port 60h; port 61h reads what was last written to it.  A program that keeps the interrupt (rather than passing it on to the previous handler) gets no keys from INT 16h or DOS until it passes one on.
- If the system has a Sound Blaster (see [SND$](../../../../bdtech/dev/#snd)), and no other V86 machine is using it, the machine borrows it, so its programs can play music and digitized sound (eg, Wolfenstein 3D): the card's ports and its FM synthesizer's (388h) are the machine's, its interrupts are the machine's, and its DMA channel works through the DMA controller's ports (00h-0Fh and 80h-8Fh), with the machine's addresses.  The card goes back when V86 ends (however it ends), and V86's own handle for it is the last of its 20, so the machine's programs get only 19 handles.
- The other I/O ports are the interrupt controller's (20h and 21h, which read as zero; an end of interrupt does nothing), the game port (201h), the parallel ports (278h, 378h, and 3BCh), and without a Sound Blaster, its ports (210h-26Fh), an FM sound card's (388h and 389h), and the DMA controller's, which read as they do when there's no such device (programs like MSBASIC read the game port on every tick).  An IN or OUT with any other port ends the program with a `CPU fault` message.  The speaker doesn't sound.
- Any other interrupt that the machine's programs don't handle themselves, other than DOS's, a breakpoint (INT 03h) or an INT 06h instruction (which do nothing without a debugger, as in real mode), and a few that only check whether something is installed (INT 28h, 2Ah, and 2Fh, and INT 33h, whose default vector points to an IRET, which tells programs that there's no mouse), ends the program with a `CPU fault` message, and so does an instruction that real mode allows but a V86 machine doesn't (eg, HLT).
- On a video console, the console's video memory is at its usual address (B8000h, or B0000h for a monochrome adapter), with the console's own text page there, as page 0 would be (whichever page the console is on), so programs can draw directly, and COMMAND.COM's graphics statements (eg, in DONKEY.BAS) work; while another console on the same adapter is in another mode (eg, after SCREEN 1), the machine's video memory is the saved copy of its console's screen (see [SCREEN](../../device/screen/#screen)), so its programs keep drawing, or if there wasn't enough memory to save it, a program that touches it waits until that console returns to its original mode.  On an EGA or VGA, a program can also set one of their own graphics modes (0Dh-13h, eg, mode 13h for Wolfenstein 3D), with INT 10h function 00h: the machine's video memory is then the 64K at A0000h, and the program can use the adapter's ports (3C0h-3DFh) directly, as it would in real mode, until it sets a text mode again.  On a VGA, Shift-Tab can switch away from such a console: the machine is suspended (it doesn't run at all, so a game stops, and a borrowed Sound Blaster pauses), and the adapter's state (its registers, palette, and all of its memory) is saved, until Shift-Tab switches back to it, which restores the state and resumes the machine (FM notes that were playing stop until the music plays its next ones).  KILL or CTRL-ALT-DEL still ends a suspended program, and its console returns to its original mode.  If there isn't enough memory to save the state (about 257K), or the adapter is an EGA, Shift-Tab can't switch away.  On a terminal, the machine has no video memory.
- The machine's BIOS data is a copy, in which only the keyboard data and the tick count are kept current.

ERRORLEVEL is set to the program's exit code, or 1 if V86 couldn't run it.  When V86 is the first program of its session (eg, `START V86`), its console closes when it ends, so if V86 or its program fails (a non-zero exit code), V86 first displays `Press any key` and waits for one, so that the messages can be read.

Source: [software/src/os/util/v86](https://github.com/jeffpar/basicdos/tree/main/software/src/os/util/v86)
